transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi. I’m here because I’ve been feeling constantly restless, like I’m wound too tight and can’t really settle down. Even in situations where I should be calm—like sitting through a planning meeting, painting, or doing yoga—I still feel like I can’t fully relax.
Do you ever get sudden surges of intense fear or discomfort that peak within a few minutes?
Not really, no. I mean, I get restless or keyed up, but I don’t think I have those sudden fear episodes that peak like that.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of different things?
I don’t think so. I mean, I worry about normal stuff sometimes, but I wouldn’t say it’s excessive or about a lot of different things.
Have there been times when your mood felt unusually high or irritable for you?
I’m not really sure. I don’t think I’ve had periods where my mood was unusually high. Irritable, maybe at times, but it feels more like normal frustration than a big shift in mood.
Did this restlessness start after a major stressful event or change in your life?

Yes, I think it got noticeably harder to manage after the conflicts with my in-laws started taking over more of our evenings. That’s been going on for about two years, maybe a little over two years now.
When the conflict with your in-laws eases up, does your restlessness also ease up?

Not really all the way. If things are quieter with them, I’m less stirred up, sure, but the restless feeling is still there. It’s like I’m wound too tight and can’t fully settle, even in situations where I should be calm, like a planning meeting, painting, or even yoga.
Did you often feel this same kind of inner restlessness when you were a child?

Yes, I think so. I remember in elementary school getting notes sent home because I kept getting out of my seat, talking over other kids, and blurting out answers before the teacher had even finished the question.
As an adult, do you still often have trouble staying seated in situations where you’re expected to remain seated?

Yes, I do. If a meeting runs long, I have a hard time just staying in my chair. I’ll find reasons to get up, like getting water or going to look at samples. And at tense family dinners, especially with my in-laws, I’ll get up to check the oven or do something in the kitchen instead of sitting there.
Do you often have trouble keeping your attention on tasks, even when you want to focus?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t paid close enough attention to that to say it happens often. Sometimes I can focus if I really need to, but I’d have to think more about whether it’s a regular problem.
Do you often make careless mistakes or miss details when you’re working on tasks?

Yes, that does happen. Over the past couple of years, I’ll think I’ve checked a vendor spreadsheet carefully, and then our planning coordinator finds something I missed—like I transposed a SKU, missed a freight surcharge, or copied the wrong quantity into the purchase order. It’s frustrating because I really do think I’ve looked it over.
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks or activities?
I’m not sure. I don’t think of myself as especially disorganized, but I haven’t really paid attention to whether organizing tasks is a frequent problem. I’d have to think about that more.
Do you often get distracted easily when you’re trying to focus on something?
I’m not sure. I mean, I can get sidetracked sometimes, but I haven’t really noticed whether it happens often when I’m trying to focus. I’d probably have to pay more attention to that.
Do you often feel like you’re driven by a motor, as if you have to keep moving even when you want to slow down?

Yes, I think so. Even on weekends, I have a hard time just stopping. I’ll finish one thing and then immediately start another—laundry, emails, reorganizing product samples, touching up a painting. My husband has said I never really power down, and that’s probably fair.
Do you often have trouble finishing tasks once the most interesting part is over?
I’m not really sure. I can think of times where I lose interest once the fun or challenging part is done, but I haven’t noticed whether it’s a regular problem for me.
Do these restlessness and attention-related problems cause significant difficulties in more than one part of your life, such as both at work and at home?

Yes, I think it does, though maybe not severely. At work, it’s led to some purchase orders needing corrections, and my planning coordinator has had to review things more closely. At home, family dinners can get tense because people feel like I’m talking over them. So yes, it does show up in more than one place.
As a child, did you often have trouble paying attention in class or when doing homework?

I’m not really sure. I don’t remember my school years clearly enough to say whether that was a regular issue. I think I got through school okay, but I can’t say for certain how much trouble I had paying attention in class or with homework.
Do you often have difficulty following through on instructions or finishing tasks after you start them?

I’m not sure I’d say often. I do sometimes start something and then it kind of stalls, especially if it’s not urgent, but I haven’t really tracked whether I fail to follow through on instructions regularly. I’d need to think about that more.
Before the conflict with your in-laws began, were you already someone who felt chronically restless or unable to fully relax?

Yes. Before all of that started, I already felt restless a lot of the time. It’s like I’m wound too tight and can’t really settle, even in situations where I’m supposed to be calm—like sitting through a planning meeting, painting, or even doing yoga. I can do those things, but I don’t feel fully relaxed.
Before age 12, did teachers or family often describe you as fidgety or unable to stay seated?

Yes, I do remember that. In elementary school I had notes sent home because I kept getting out of my seat, talking over other kids, and blurting out answers before the teacher had even finished asking the question.
Do you often interrupt other people or finish their sentences before they’re done?

Yes, I do that. At work especially, I’ll catch myself jumping into junior buyers’ conversations to correct some detail or add my opinion before they’ve really asked for it. I’m usually trying to be helpful, not take over, but I know it can come across like I’m interrupting.

final_diagnosis.reason: The presentation is most consistent with ADHD, predominantly hyperactive/impulsive type: chronic restlessness predating recent stressors, clear childhood onset before age 12, persistent adult symptoms of hyperactivity/impulsivity, and impairment across work and home. Adjustment disorder was considered because symptoms worsened during prolonged conflict with in-laws, but the symptoms clearly existed beforehand and do not resolve with reduced stress. Unspecified anxiety disorder is less likely because the patient denies excessive generalized worry and panic-like episodes, and the core syndrome is lifelong hyperactive/impulsive restlessness rather than anxiety.
